what: The hub and two motors ride on a platform with a free vertical bearing. Motor A turns a balanced reaction wheel. Motor B moves two balanced masses inward and outward. Watch the platform heading after the masses and both motor angles return to their starting values. The sequence of internal movements can matter even when the final internal shape looks the same.
try: Load afterturn.ldr and afterturn.bw. Use Reset to restore the saved pose, then press Run in Robot Lab’s toolbar. Identify the free platform, the reaction wheel and the two movable masses.

Follow the first closed cycle: B moves to 70° to bring the masses inward, A turns to 900°, B returns the masses outward, then A returns to 0°. Compare the platform with the lower support during the first held checkpoint.
Watch the inverse sequence. Predict whether changing the order should add to or undo the first platform turn. Check the actual mass positions as well as the encoders.
Load afterturn-fixed-masses.ldr and run the same supplied program from Reset. Compare the net platform turn with the moving-mass model, while checking that the driven motions complete.

Reset before repeating after a manual move, interruption or completed experiment. The internal home is not automatically the platform’s original heading. Keep the supplied finite program and operating bounds.
why: A motor exchanges angular momentum between its rotor and its support. At a fixed mass radius, the platform’s response to a wheel turn depends on the complete rotating assembly’s inertia. Moving the balanced masses changes that inertia. Turning the wheel one way with the masses inward and back with them outward therefore need not produce equal and opposite platform turns. Returning the internal configuration is different from returning the orientation of the whole assembly.
matters: A mechanism can change its orientation through an ordered cycle of internal motions without a motor directly driving its support bearing. This is a simple setting for geometric phase: the path through internal configurations matters. It also shows why successful encoder homing alone cannot certify an object’s global pose.
question: If both encoders read their starting values and the masses return to their outer positions, must the platform face its original direction? What should happen when the same wheel motion is performed with the masses fixed?
answer: No. With moving masses, the wheel’s outward and return turns occur at different inertias, so their platform rotations need not cancel. If the masses stay fixed, that difference is removed and the ideal reciprocal wheel turns cancel. The useful comparison is the independently observed net heading with matched completed inputs; damping, initial motion and finite return errors must still be measured. In the supplied finite native run, the movable-mass platform retained 4.6625° after the first cycle and 0.0261° after the inverse; the fixed-mass comparison retained 0.0037° after its first cycle. These are native observations, not measured LEGO hardware accuracy.
further: Sketch the actual reaction-wheel angle on one axis and the mean observed mass radius on the other. The selected nominal radii are 51.056819 mm inside and 64 mm outside. Reversing the order reverses the enclosed path. The supplied bounded shape stroke is 70°, not a full crank revolution.
Compare with Counterturn and Momentum Twins. Those examples exchange angular momentum at fixed inertia; Afterturn changes the internal configuration between the wheel’s forward and return strokes.
The motors supply energy. A final orientation change at small total angular momentum is not energy creation, friction-free perpetual motion or gyroscopic precession.

The prediction must include the real motor assemblies, hub, slider masses and shape-drive links. Bearing damping, support motion and cable forces can affect a finite experiment. Native results are not a hardware precision or load rating.

Keep the supplied hub shelf and balance trim in place. A tilted bearing and an off-centre carried mass can add a gravity torque, so a free bearing alone does not guarantee an isolated angular-momentum experiment.
formula: Ideal held-shape segment: Δψ ≈ −Iw·Δα/Jlocked(r). ψ is platform yaw relative to the base, α is wheel angle relative to the platform, Iw is wheel axial inertia, and Jlocked(r) is the complete yaw inertia with internal motions locked at radius r. For an inner-radius wheel turn +Δα and an outer-radius return −Δα, Δψcycle ≈ −Iw·Δα·[1/Jinner − 1/Jouter]. This simplified planning relation assumes negligible external yaw torque. The complete prediction also includes the angular momentum of the moving shape-drive parts; observed yaw is measured from body poses, not generated by the formula. The formula uses a common positive axis for α and ψ. In this model, the native A axis is opposite the reported positive platform-yaw axis, so α = −A for the plotted input.
